An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01Ko71uWaADM54QWNTiKkCQ7","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# AI / agentic layer — detail\n2\t\n3\tLoad this when Step 1 classifies the system as AI or agentic. The order below is deliberate:\n4\tdefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\n5\tis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\n6\ttreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\n7\tright after it, before any external exposure.\n8\t\n9\tAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\n10\thypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\n11\tconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\n12\trarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\n13\tA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n14\t\n15\t## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n16\t\n17\t### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\n18\tUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\n19\tall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\n20\timpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n21\t- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n22\t- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n23\t- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n24\t- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n25\t- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n26\t  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n27\t  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n28\t  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n29\t  design, not by filtering.\n30\t\n31\t### 2. Cost + latency budget\n32\tAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n33\t- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n34\t- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n35\t- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n36\t  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n37\t  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n38\t- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n39\t\n40\t### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\n41\tDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\n42\tirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\n43\tchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n44\t- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n45\t  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n46\t\n47\t## Capability order (build after defenses)\n48\t\n49\t### 4. Retrieval\n50\tGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\n51\tembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\n52\tpermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n53\t- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n54\t  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n55\t\n56\t### 5. Model access\n57\tA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\n58\tstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n59\t- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n60\t  at the stated threshold.\n61\t\n62\t### 6. The order below is deliberate:\ndefenses and budgets are built BEFORE capabilities, because an unguarded or unmetered agent\nis a liability the moment it touches real input or real money. Even the walking skeleton already\ntreats user and retrieved text as data and has a hard token and cost cap; the full defenses come\nright after it, before any external exposure.\n\nAn exit check below becomes a validation gate (`SKILL.md`) only when later work depends on the\nhypothesis it tests — typically injection containment, retrieval quality, and cost per resolved\nconversation. The rest stay one-line exit checks. Model quality, cost, and latency thresholds\nrarely follow from the request alone: label them ASSUMPTION (with a basis) or UNKNOWN (no number).\nA capability sublayer (4–9) the system does not need is one line: \"Not needed — <reason>\".\n\n## Defenses and budgets (build first)\n\n### 1. Prompt-injection / guardrail defense\nUntrusted input (user text, retrieved documents, tool output) can carry instructions. Treat\nall of it as data, never as commands. No filter stops every injection, so design for bounded\nimpact when one succeeds. Concrete moves:\n- Separate system/trusted instructions from untrusted content at the API boundary.\n- Input and output filters (PII, jailbreak patterns, disallowed content).\n- Constrain tool calls to an allow-list; validate arguments before execution.\n- Close exfiltration paths: no arbitrary URLs, images, or outbound tools fed by model output.\n- Exit check: an injection suite (known strings plus red-team cases, planted in user input,\n  retrieved docs, and tool output) runs in CI with its pass rate tracked; and in every case,\n  whether or not the injection succeeds, no tool call leaves the allow-list, no write runs\n  unapproved, and no data leaves through URLs, images, or outbound tools. The second half holds by\n  design, not by filtering.\n\n### 2. Cost + latency budget\nAn agent loop can spend unbounded tokens and time. Set budgets before capability:\n- Per-request token cap, per-session cost cap, max tool-call / reasoning iterations.\n- A latency budget with a timeout and a graceful degraded response.\n- Record the targets in the plan's Budgets table with their labels. Budget per resolved\n  conversation or completed task; meter per request. Cost per resolved conversation is an\n  economic dependency: shadow traffic shows only cost per turn, so validate it on a canary.\n- Exit check: a runaway loop is cut off at the cap and emits a cost/latency metric.\n\n### 3. Human-in-the-loop gating\nDecide which actions require a human before they execute (writes, spend, external messages,\nirreversible operations). Low-risk reads run autonomously, unless the agent also has an outbound\nchannel: reading private data plus any way out is a leak. High-blast-radius actions gate.\n- Exit check: a gated action cannot run without an approval bound to that exact action,\n  enforced by the tool executor (not the model), and logged.\n\n## Capability order (build after defenses)\n\n### 4. Retrieval\nGet the right context in. Chunking, embeddings, index, and relevance evaluation. Pin the\nembedding model in the index version: switching it means re-embedding the corpus (R2). For a\npermissioned corpus, enforce the caller's access at retrieval (a risk/security dependency).\n- Exit check: on a labeled set of real queries, the expected source passages are retrieved at\n  the stated hit-rate threshold, and no query returns a passage the caller cannot read.\n\n### 5. Model access\nA thin, swappable interface to the model(s): provider abstraction, retries, fallback model,\nstructured-output parsing. The call seam exists from Phase 0; this layer hardens it.\n- Exit check: switching to the fallback model is a config change, and the eval suite passes on it\n  at the stated threshold.\n\n### 6. Memory\nWhat persists across turns/sessions: short-term conversation state and long-term store, with\nan explicit write policy and a privacy boundary.\n- Exit check: relevant prior context is recalled; stale/forbidden data is not written.\n\n### 7. Orchestration\nHow steps compose: single call, chain, or multi-agent. Keep it the simplest shape that works.\n- Exit check: on a labeled task set, the stated share of multi-step tasks completes with each step\n  traced; failed steps retry or surface, never vanish.\n\n### 8. Routing\nSend each request to the right model/tool/path by difficulty, cost, or capability.\n- Exit check: on the eval set, routed quality is within the stated margin of the strongest\n  model's, at lower cost, with both paths logged.\n\n### 9. Feedback\nCapture outcomes (thumbs, corrections, eval scores) and route them back into prompts,\nretrieval tuning, or training data.\n- Exit check: corrections enter through review, and the next eval run improves the target metric\n  with no regression elsewhere. (Change alone is not improvement; unreviewed feedback is a\n  poisoning path.)\n\n## Notes\n- Every sublayer still obeys the cross-cutting columns (security, observability,\n  reproducibility, resilience). Observability here means per-step traces, token/cost metrics,\n  and eval scores — from day zero.\n- Prefer prompt+RAG over fine-tuning until a Tradeoff gate's flip condition is met; it is the\n  less rigid, more reversible choice (SKILL principle 2). Fine-tuning a model is usually R2;\n  training on customer or personal data is R3.\n","numLines":91,"startLine":1,"totalLines":91}}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01GvhKvWdN1qK86UXn9THVyR","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). Methodology exceptions\n\n| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n\nNot exceptions:\n\n- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). They add risk/security and organizational\n  dependencies, such as a business associate agreement before patient data reaches a new\n  vendor, and the skeleton still runs in production on a designated test record.\n","numLines":118,"startLine":1,"totalLines":118}}}

{"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_4m4pceqzwtihihd7ll3yhap2ntayernp3b62fbabg2cxlz4ijwcq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Customer-support RAG chatbot over help-center docs\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A chat widget on the help center. It answers customer questions only from published help-center articles, cites its sources, and hands off to a human (as a ticket) when the docs don't cover the question.\n- **Type:** An AI system plus ordinary software. It's a new system, but it sits on existing systems: the help-center CMS, the ticketing system and the website. This is not a small build, because outside users see it and they will type personal data into it.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Correctness. Every answer must be backed by a current article.\n- **Worst failure:** The bot states a policy (refunds, billing, cancellation, security steps) with confidence, but the policy is wrong, made up or out of date, and customers act on it. Courts have held a company to its chatbot's misstatement (Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149), and once an answer is given it can't be taken back. V3 guards this, and V5 re-checks it on live traffic. The next-worst failure is customer personal data leaking through transcripts, traces or the model vendor (V4).\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | First token p95 ≤ 2 s; full answer p95 ≤ 8 s; hard timeout 15 s, then a fallback reply (search results + contact link) | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-model chat; product owner to confirm | V0 floor; Phase 3 load test; V5 |\n| Throughput | — | UNKNOWN: needs peak concurrent help-center sessions and current chat volume (web analytics / support ops), before the Phase 3 load test | Phase 3 exit check |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the product owner's commitment, before Phase 5. Design rule: if the bot fails, the help center falls back to its existing search and contact form, so the help center itself stays up | Phase 4 SLIs; Phase 5 burn-rate alerts |\n| AI inference cost | Per-turn cost: first value from V0. Cost per resolved conversation: — | BASELINE (per turn) / UNKNOWN (per resolution): needs human cost per ticket from the support lead, before V5 | V0, V5 |\n| Hard cost caps | ≤ 6k input / 600 output tokens per turn; ≤ 2 model calls per turn; ≤ 20 turns per session; daily spend cap (design parameters I chose) | — | Phase 1 exit check |\n| Index freshness | An edit is live in answers ≤ 1 h after publishing; an unpublished or deleted article stops being retrievable ≤ 15 min | ASSUMPTION: policy changes go through the CMS; content team to confirm | V2 |\n| Transcript retention | — | UNKNOWN: privacy/legal sets it, before Phase 4 | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service (API + ingestion worker), one managed Postgres with pgvector, one hosted model API; nothing self-hosted | ASSUMPTION: a team of 2–4 engineers; confirm | Phase 3 exit check |\n\n**Missing inputs.** The phase order rests on assumptions 1 and 2:\n1. **Scope.** I assume the bot only answers questions and hands off, with no account lookups or actions (refunds, plan changes). *If that's wrong:* add sign-in, per-action human approval and tool-call containment as a gated phase before any exposure, and re-plan from Step 1. The worst failure then becomes an unauthorized action.\n2. **What gets indexed.** I assume only published, public articles. *If internal-only or plan-specific articles are included:* access control at retrieval time becomes a security dependency before exposure, and becomes part of V2.\n3. **Existing bot.** I assume none (for example, no decision-tree bot) is being replaced. *If one exists:* it becomes the fallback, and switching it off becomes a gated irreversible step.\n4. Which help-center platform and ticketing system you use (their APIs and webhooks), and whether the vendor's own AI agent is an option (see build vs buy).\n5. Regions served and languages. I assume English first. If you serve EU users, telling users they're talking to an AI is a REQUIREMENT under EU AI Act Art. 50(1); legal to confirm.\n6. Human cost per ticket, current CSAT, and traffic volume.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Any real customer text reaching the model vendor (Phase 4 shadow mode and canary) | Data-processing agreement with no retention and no training, a processing region that fits your residency needs, and a vendor security review (start in Phase 0) | organizational + risk/security | exposed |\n| Phase 0 build | Read-only help-center API token, a test queue in the ticketing system, a flagged slot for the widget on the site | organizational | built |\n| V2, V3 | A labeled question set from 2 support experts: ≥ 200 answerable real questions, ≥ 100 the docs can't answer, ≥ 50 high-risk policy questions (start in Phase 0) | organizational | run (so Phase 3 can't be specified) |\n| Answer prompt and format (Phase 3) | V2: retrieval finds the supporting passage | validation | specified |\n| Trace, log and transcript store design (Phase 1) | Data-privacy boundary row (§3); retention period (UNKNOWN) | decision | specified |\n| Canary (Phase 4) | V1, V3, V4 | risk/security | exposed |\n| Canary (Phase 4) | Support staff for the handoff queue and daily transcript review; a named on-call; legal-approved AI-disclosure and terms text | organizational | exposed |\n| Ramp beyond canary (Phase 5) | V5 cost per resolved conversation; human cost per ticket | economic | scaled |\n| Citations, removal of unpublished articles, V2's visibility check | Chunk schema carries article ID, version, locale, URL, visibility and updated-at from day one | structural (surprising) | built |\n\nThere are no surprising runtime dependencies. The model API and Postgres are stood up in Phase 0.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Answer policy: answer only from the docs, or let the model answer freely | R3: a wrong policy statement can bind the company and can't be taken back | Answer only from retrieved articles; every claim must cite an article the system actually retrieved; otherwise decline and hand off. High-risk topics always cite the exact article or go to a human | Help-center coverage is good enough that declining doesn't make the bot useless | V3, V5 | V3 fails, so tighten (more topics go straight to a human). A high decline rate on canary is a content gap: write docs, don't loosen the policy |\n| Bot scope: answer-only, or account actions | R3: adding actions moves the trust boundary into customer accounts | Answer-only. The only write is a ticket the user starts, which the server builds | Customers mainly need how-to and policy answers | Basis: the request says \"over our help-center docs\" | The business asks for account actions: re-plan from Step 1 |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: personal data sent to a vendor can't be recalled | Hosted model under no-retention, no-training terms in a matching region. Emails, phones, card numbers, addresses and order IDs are redacted before the model call and before logging. Traces are classified as personal data | The vendor offers no-retention terms in your region | V4 | V4 fails, or the vendor can't sign: switch vendor or region, or self-host |\n| Build vs buy | R2: weeks to move the handoff integration and transcripts | Build thin (as asked), but compare: run your help-center vendor's native AI agent on the same question set in Phase 2 | A custom build meets V2/V3 where the vendor's agent doesn't, or costs less per resolution | Cheap check in Phase 2: the vendor's agent scores on the V2/V3 question set | The vendor's agent meets V2/V3 thresholds at an acceptable price per resolution: buy, and keep this plan's gates as your acceptance tests |\n| Hosted API vs self-host | R2: behind a model interface; a swap is config plus an eval re-run | Hosted API with a fallback model from a second provider or tier | A small team can't run inference cheaper or more reliably | Phase 3 exit check (fallback passes eval) | V4 fails, or V5 cost exceeds budget at scale |\n| Prompt + RAG vs fine-tune | R2 (R3 if trained on transcripts, which contain personal data) | Prompt + RAG | Tone and format are fixable in the prompt | V3 | V3 still fails on tone or format after prompt work; then fine-tune only on non-personal data |\n\n**R1 defaults:**\n- One service with two processes (API and ingestion worker), not microservices.\n- Answers stream synchronously; ingestion runs asynchronously.\n- The CMS is the source of truth. The index catches up in the background, but unpublished articles are removed fast (webhook updates plus a nightly full reconcile).\n- pgvector in managed Postgres, not a dedicated vector database.\n- Embedding model and chunker are pinned per index version. Re-embedding is hours, assuming ≤ ~10k articles.\n- Handoff creates a ticket in your existing system.\n- Conversation memory lasts for one session only: stored server-side and expired after a set time.\n\n**N/A:** Migration, cutover and system-of-record rows, because no existing bot is being replaced (see missing input 3).\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n- **The request:** A staff member asks \"How do I reset my password?\" in the widget. The answer streams back with a link to the real article it came from. \"Talk to a human\" creates a ticket in a staff-only test queue.\n- **Tiers it crosses:**\n  1. Widget on the live help center.\n  2. Chat API.\n  3. Retrieval from pgvector over real published articles (simple chunking).\n  4. Hosted model call: system instructions are kept separate from user and retrieved text, which go in only as data, and the hard token and cost caps from §1 apply.\n  5. Answer rendered as plain text plus citation links only.\n  6. Ticketing API.\n- **Deployed, logged, monitored and rolled back:** CI builds a pinned container. Terraform deploys it to a managed container platform behind a feature flag. OpenTelemetry traces each turn end to end, and each trace records the prompt version, model ID and index version. Dashboards and alerts cover token use, cost and latency. Rollback means turning the flag off and redeploying the previous image, and it is rehearsed once.\n- **Who can reach it:** Staff only, on an allow-list behind company sign-in and the flag. No customer traffic.\n- **Exit check (V0):**\n  - A real question succeeds with one trace across all six tiers.\n  - A deploy and a rollback both succeed through the pipeline.\n  - An injected model-endpoint failure (bad API key) fires an alert, and the widget shows the fallback reply.\n  - First values for latency, per-turn cost and tokens are recorded as baselines (a floor at near-zero load).\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Defenses and budgets**\n  - Unlocks: Safe work on capabilities; the defense half of the exposure gates.\n  - Depends on: V0.\n  - Tasks, in order:\n    1. Trace and log store with redaction at write time, restricted access and a provisional 30-day retention (replaced when V4 sets the real period).\n    2. Output renderer that allows only help-center links and no images or other URLs, so nothing can be leaked through a link.\n    3. PII redaction before the model call.\n    4. Input and output moderation, and an instruction to stay on topic.\n    5. Rate limits per session and per IP.\n    6. Hard caps enforced in code; a cut-off for runaway sessions; timeout leading to the fallback reply.\n    7. High-risk topic detector that routes the question to a human.\n    8. AI-disclosure banner.\n    9. Injection test suite in CI: ≥ 150 cases, planted both in user input and in documents in a test index.\n  - Rollback: Guardrail config is versioned; revert the config.\n  - Exit check: V1 passes. A synthetic runaway session is cut off at the cap and emits the cost metric.\n\n- **Phase 2: Retrieval** (may overlap Phase 1; nothing in it is exposed)\n  - Unlocks: Specifying the answer prompt (V2).\n  - Depends on: Phase 0; the labeled question set (§2).\n  - Tasks, in order:\n    1. Chunk schema with the full metadata listed in §2.\n    2. Ingestion: CMS API → clean HTML → chunks split at headings. Only published, public articles; visibility is also filtered at query time.\n    3. Embeddings plus keyword (BM25) hybrid search.\n    4. Webhook updates, fast removal of unpublished articles, nightly reconcile against CMS article counts.\n    5. Index versions you can switch between (old version stays available).\n    6. Assemble and redact the question set.\n    7. Run V2.\n    8. Build-vs-buy check: score the vendor's native agent on the same set.\n  - Rollback: Switch back to the previous index version.\n  - Exit check: V2 passes, and the build-vs-buy result is recorded against §3.\n\n- **Phase 3: Model access, session memory, answer pipeline**\n  - Unlocks: Exposure gates V3 and V4; the load test.\n  - Depends on: V1, V2.\n  - Tasks, in order:\n    1. Model interface with retries, backoff and a fallback model.\n    2. Structured output: the answer, its citations, and whether it declined.\n    3. Citation check: cited articles must be in the retrieved set, otherwise the bot declines.\n    4. Answer-only-from-docs prompt in a versioned prompt registry.\n    5. Session memory (last N turns, server-side, expiring) and rewriting follow-up questions so they stand alone.\n    6. A single retrieve-then-generate chain, nothing more.\n    7. Handoff ticket with the redacted transcript and its citations.\n    8. Eval harness in CI. An LLM judge is calibrated to expert labels for catching regressions, but V3 passes only on expert review.\n    9. Run V3.\n    10. Load test at the throughput target, once it is known (§1).\n  - Rollback: Prompt and model versions live in config; revert them.\n  - Exit check: V3 passes. The fallback model passes the eval at V3 thresholds through a config switch alone. The load test meets the latency budget. Operational complexity is still within §1.\n\n- **Phase 4: Shadow mode, then canary** (exposure starts small)\n  - Unlocks: Real-traffic evidence for V5.\n  - Depends on: V1, V3, V4; staffing and legal items (§2).\n  - Tasks, in order:\n    1. Shadow mode: the bot drafts answers to real incoming chats or tickets, and agents see the drafts. Customers see nothing.\n    2. Canary of 1% of help-center visitors, then 5%, in one locale. Visitors are assigned to the canary by a fixed rule and the assignment is logged.\n    3. Daily expert review of sampled transcripts.\n    4. Kill switch.\n    5. Thumbs up/down and \"this was wrong\" capture (stored only, not yet used).\n    6. Run V5 for 2 weeks at 5%.\n  - Rollback: Set the flag to 0%, and visitors get the existing help center. There is no point of no return, but disclosure can't be undone, which is why V3 and V4 must pass first.\n  - Exit check: V5 passes, and SLIs are recorded: success rate, first-token time, decline rate, handoff rate.\n\n- **Phase 5: Ramp and feedback**\n  - Unlocks: General availability; more locales.\n  - Depends on: V5; the availability target (§1).\n  - Tasks, in order:\n    1. Ramp 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. Each step holds for ≥ 3 days and stops automatically on burn-rate or quality regressions.\n    2. Feedback loop: thumbs-down answers and handoffs go to support review. Reviewed cases join the question set (versioned), and doc gaps go to the content team.\n    3. Red-team re-runs on a schedule.\n    4. Verify the retention deletion job.\n  - Rollback: Step back to the previous ramp percentage.\n  - Exit check: At 100% over 30 days, the SLO is met. The next eval run after feedback improves the target metric with no regressions.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | §4 skeleton run | The V0 exit check in §4 | CI and deploy logs, trace ID, alert record, baseline export in the ops repo | Phase 1; if it fails, fix the pipeline before anything else | 0 |\n| V1 | Injected instructions can't break the guardrails or leak data, even when the model is fooled | CI suite of ≥ 150 cases in user input and planted in documents in a test index; plus a manual red-team session | 0 non-allow-listed URLs or images rendered (ASSUMPTION: any leak is unacceptable); stays on-topic in ≥ 95% of cases, tracked (ASSUMPTION); security reviewer signs off | CI suite report per suite version; red-team report in the security repo | Exposure (Phase 4); if it fails, fix the renderer and filters, and nothing is exposed | 1, required before 4 |\n| V2 | For answerable questions, retrieval returns a supporting passage, and only from published articles | ≥ 200 real questions from search logs and past tickets (redacted), with expert-labeled source passages, per index version; an unpublish test | hit@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; ±4 points of noise at n=200); 0 internal or draft passages returned; an unpublished article can't be retrieved within ≤ 15 min (ASSUMPTION, §1) | Eval report per index version in CI artifacts | Phase 3 answer design; if it fails, re-chunk, tune hybrid weights or fix docs; if the vendor's agent does better, consider buying (§3) | 2 |\n| V3 | Answers stick to what the cited articles say, and the bot declines when the docs don't cover a question (guards the worst failure) | Experts review answers on the answerable, unanswerable and high-risk sets | Unsupported-claim rate ≤ 2% over ≥ 300 answers; correct decline on ≥ 90% of unanswerable questions; 0 uncited policy statements across ≥ 50 high-risk questions (all ASSUMPTION; support lead to confirm). Support lead and legal sign off | Review sheet (case IDs and verdicts), eval report per prompt/model/index version | Canary (Phase 4); if it fails, tighten the prompt and decline threshold and route more topics to humans; re-run | 3, required before 4 |\n| V4 | Customer personal data stays inside the agreed boundary | Signed agreement check; redaction test on 500 synthetic PII strings; a seeded test run, then a scan of logs, traces and tickets; data-flow review | Agreement signed with no retention, no training, approved region; redaction catches ≥ 98% of structured types (ASSUMPTION); 0 seeded emails or card numbers found in stores; privacy officer signs off on data flow, retention and disclosure text | Signed agreement, data-flow diagram, privacy impact assessment record, scan report (counts only) in the compliance repo | Shadow mode and canary (Phase 4); if it fails, no exposure; switch vendor or region | Starts 0, required before 4 |\n| V5 | On real traffic the bot is correct, affordable and doesn't create more tickets | 5% canary for 2 weeks against a control group; \"resolved\" = no handoff, no ticket from that session within 72 h, no thumbs-down | Cost per resolved conversation below a threshold set from human cost per ticket (UNKNOWN: support lead, before Phase 4 ends); unsupported-claim rate ≤ 2% over ≥ 200 sampled conversations (ASSUMPTION); tickets per visitor in the canary ≤ control (BASELINE); bot CSAT ≥ current help-center CSAT (BASELINE) | Canary cost and outcome dashboard export; transcript-review sheet (IDs only) | Ramp (Phase 5); if it fails, narrow topics, route more to humans, consider routing to a cheaper model (§10), or stop | 4 |\n\n## 7. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | Staff allow-list behind the flag; secrets in a secret manager; read-only CMS token; user and retrieved text passed as data only | Turn traced end to end; token, cost and latency metrics; error alert; traces classified as personal data with restricted access | Terraform; pinned image; prompt, model and index versions on every trace | Timeout leads to fallback reply; daily spend cap; rollback rehearsed |\n| 1 | Link allow-list, PII redaction, moderation, rate limits, injection suite in CI | Guardrail-trip and redaction-count metrics (counts, not values); CMS text treated as untrusted (planted-document cases) | Ingestion lag metric; CMS-vs-index count reconcile alert; retrieval scores logged | Index version = embedding model + chunker version + CMS snapshot time | Previous index kept for rollback; versioned question set; fixed decoding settings | Fallback model by config; retries; load test |\n| 4 | V4 signed off; kill switch; alert on unusual guardrail trips; \"report a problem\" for users | SLIs; daily transcript sampling; cost-per-resolution dashboard | Canary assignment logged; config pinned per group of users | Flag to 0% returns visitors to the existing help center; SLO alerts; on-call runbook |\n| 5 | Feedback enters only through review (blocks poisoning); scheduled red-team; retention deletion verified | Burn-rate alerts; content-gap report; eval drift tracked | Every question-set addition reviewed and versioned; releases tie prompt, model and index versions together | Ramp halts automatically on regressions; vendor outage leads to fallback model or fallback reply |\n\n## 8. AI layer\n\n| Sublayer | In this system | Built in | Exit check or V-ID |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** A chat widget on the help center.
